fig-med-01.alt: Single-layer figs drying on outdoor trays in Morocco
fig-med-01.caption: Sarılop on open trays—the kerevet rule (single layer, sun and air) in an Aydın-style fig drying yard on the Büyük Menderes plain, Türkiye; tray method photographed in Morocco.

fig-med-02.alt: Fig drying trays covered with cloth against night dew
fig-med-02.caption: Covering piled trays after dusk so dew does not undo the day’s sun— the evening rhythm of İncirliova and Germencik yards on the Menderes.

fig-med-03.commons: File:Fig. 1. Cella vinaria. Fig. 2. Raccolta dei fichi. Fig. 3. Raccolta delle bamie (NYPL b14291206-425529).tiff
fig-med-03.alt: 19th-century engraving of fig harvest and drying in Calabria, Italy
fig-med-03.caption: Passuluni and cannizze country—historical Calabrian fig harvest and field drying (Fichi di Cosenza hinterland), from NYPL via Wikimedia Commons.

fig-med-04.alt: Graded dried figs including paired askada-style packs
fig-med-04.caption: Askades of Kymi—paired, pressed dried fig faces from Evia’s xira syka PDO trade (illustrative graded dried figs).

fig-med-05.alt: String of dried figs hanging to air in storage
fig-med-05.caption: Winter necklaces—dried figs strung on rafters and wires across Aegean and Anatolian storerooms before the tin.
fig-med-05.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Dried figs (2).jpg (CC0); illustrative strung/air-dried storage.

fig-med-06.alt: Historical scientific illustration of the fig wasp Blastophaga psenes
fig-med-06.caption: Caprification’s worker—Blastophaga psenes on caprifig fruit, the pollination secret behind Smyrna-type orchards and Sarılop drying belts.

fig-med-07.commons_secondary: File:California a guide to the Golden state - Figs in the Dry Yard.jpg
fig-med-07.alt: Historic cargo ships at Smyrna (İzmir) harbor
fig-med-07.alt_secondary: California figs spread in a dry yard for Calimyrna curing
fig-med-07.caption: Smyrna to Calimyrna—İzmir harbor freight (Library of Congress) and a California dry yard for the same cultivar carried west (WPA guide photo, Commons).
fig-med-07.credit: LOC / Wikimedia Commons; California dry-yard photo via Commons.

fig-med-08.alt: Dalmatian dried smokve figs on slatted trays
fig-med-08.caption: Sea-dip and bay—smokve on lijese slats, Dalmatian island drying before the tin (Vis and Hvar foodway).

fig-med-09.alt: Figs drying inside a greenhouse-style tunnel
fig-med-09.caption: When August fails—tunnel and glass essiccatoio drying that rescues the crop from rain and humidity across the Mediterranean.

fig-med-10.alt: Turkish hoşaf compote with dried figs, apricots, and plums
fig-med-10.caption: Winter paste and stores—dried figs in hoşaf and the dark preserves (pestil, pekmez, matboukh) that outlive fresh season.

fig-med-11.alt: Sorted piles of export-grade dried figs
fig-med-11.caption: Grade by count—hands over sized piles and Aydın export crates where pieces-per-kilo is law, not marketing.

fig-med-12.alt: Common fig fruit on the tree in Turkish orchard
fig-med-12.caption: The fig that falls—Sarılop left to drop for drying harvest on the Büyük Menderes, contrasted in text with scissor-cut Kymi askades.
fig-med-12.credit: Wikimedia Commons — İncir / Ficus carica orchard photo.

fig-med-13.alt: Historic map of Aydın Vilayet including İncirliova fig country
fig-med-13.caption: İncirliova and the fig valley—Aydın Vilayet on an Ottoman map when rail and market street carried Sarılop to the world.

fig-med-14.alt: 19th-century painting of Smyrna harbor and shipping
fig-med-14.caption: Smyrna steamers—Levant cargo at İzmir rıhtım when dried figs rode holds east, not cruise postcards.
fig-med-14.credit: Marius Bauer, Rijksmuseum (public domain) via Wikimedia Commons.

fig-med-15.alt: Fresh Sarılop-type figs on the branch in Aydın country
fig-med-15.caption: Altın İncir festival season—Sarılop on the tree in İncirliova when stalls still sell fruit, not only the stage.
fig-med-15.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Common fig / İncir orchard.

fig-med-16.alt: Dried fruit and figs at an Athens street market stall
fig-med-16.caption: Athens laiki in August—dried figs and summer fruit at a neighborhood market stall (fresh syka in season at the same tables).
fig-med-16.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Dried fruit at Athens market.jpg.

fig-med-17.commons: File:Ballarò, puesto de fruta, Palermo, Sicilia, Italia, 2015.JPG
fig-med-17.alt: Palermo Ballarò market street with produce stalls
fig-med-17.caption: Ballarò first figs—early-hour Palermo market where common Ficus carica arrives, not fico d’India (see draft 45).

fig-med-18.alt: Capucins market hall in Marseille with North African produce
fig-med-18.caption: Marseille Noailles and Capucins—dried-fruit and fig trade between Provence and the Maghreb in the Vieux-Port hinterland.
fig-med-18.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Marché des Capucins Marseille.jpg.

fig-med-19.commons: File:Spices on Spice Bazaar in Istanbul 02.jpg
fig-med-19.alt: Spice and dried-goods stalls under Istanbul Egyptian Bazaar vaults
fig-med-19.caption: Mısır Çarşısı—the Egyptian Bazaar vaults where incir sits beside dried fruit and nuts, scoops in the bins.

fig-med-20.alt: La Boqueria market in Barcelona with summer fruit stalls
fig-med-20.caption: La Boqueria before the aisle fills—Catalan higos and late-summer flats on the Rambla market.

fig-med-21.alt: Dried figs with walnuts and cheese in a Moroccan souk
fig-med-21.caption: Fès and the western Maghreb—dried fig cones beside walnuts in the souk dried-fruit trade.
fig-med-21.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Figs, berries and cheese.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0).

fig-med-22.alt: Naxos island harbor with cargo and ferry traffic
fig-med-22.caption: Island harbor crates—Cyclades ports where fig flats wait in tarp shade before the ferry.

fig-med-23.commons: File:Holy Apostles church ancient agora from Acropolis Athens.jpg
fig-med-23.alt: Ruins of the Ancient Agora of Athens
fig-med-23.caption: Classical Athens agora—where sykon and sycophant tied the fig to market law and political insult.
fig-med-23.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Ancient Agora of Athens.

fig-med-24.commons: File:Seven Species in a painting on ceramic tiles on a street in Jerusalem.jpg
fig-med-24.alt: Tu Bishvat plate with the seven species including figs
fig-med-24.caption: Tu Bishvat shivat haminim—the fig among seven species on a holiday plate in Jewish Mediterranean kitchens.

fig-med-25.alt: Pressed develah fig cake cut to show the mash
fig-med-25.caption: Develah—pressed fig cake in the Levantine gift and wage economy of dried fruit (biblical and modern tables).

fig-med-26.alt: Calabrian crocette fig sweets with visible nuts
fig-med-26.caption: Calabrian Christmas crocette—burned-tray Fichi di Cosenza confections with nut showing, not only dipped SKU.

fig-med-27.commons: File:Ma'amoul Filled with Dates and Nuts.jpg
fig-med-27.alt: Maamoul cookies with wooden mold and filled center
fig-med-27.caption: Eid maamoul—wooden mold and broken cookie; Levantine teen (fig) paste filling, not date alone.
fig-med-27.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Ma'amoul Filled with Dates and Nuts.jpg.

fig-med-28.alt: Fresh Mediterranean figs on a Ferragosto summer table
fig-med-28.caption: Ferragosto first figs—Assumption-week bowls of fresh figs on an Italian summer table before the wasps win.
fig-med-28.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Fresh figs on a plate.jpg.

fig-med-29.alt: Turkish kuruyemiş dried fruit shop display with figs
fig-med-29.caption: Wedding and celebration trays—Anatolian kuruyemiş counters where sugared figs join dried fruit for feasts.
fig-med-29.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Kuruyemişçi at Ankara.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0, E4024).

fig-med-30.commons: File:Dried fruit at GUM Market in Yerevan, Armenia.jpg
fig-med-30.alt: Orthodox-style dried fruit bowl with figs and nuts
fig-med-30.caption: Orthodox dried-fruit bowls—figs among walnuts on a winter table (illustrative Caucasus market display).
fig-med-30.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Dried fruit at GUM Market, Yerevan.

fig-med-31.alt: Fig drying yard trays under practical night work light
fig-med-31.caption: Harvest night on the Menderes—yard trays when Sarılop comes in after dusk (same single-layer drying yard).

fig-med-32.caption: Carnival fried sweets beside Lenten restraint—chiacchiere season before plain dried-fig fast-day plates.

fig-med-33.alt: Charoset paste with visible fig for Passover Seder
fig-med-33.caption: Charoset with figs—Mediterranean Jewish Seder bowls with brown fruit paste and visible seed.
fig-med-33.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Charoset.jpg (GFDL 1.2 — verify relicensing at publish).

fig-med-34.alt: Dalmatian smokve dried figs and smokvenjak loaf
fig-med-34.caption: Smokvenjak hib—Vis and Dalmatian smokve with bay leaves, sliced loaf showing fig and walnut.

fig-med-35.alt: Andalusian pan de higo pressed fig and almond cake
fig-med-35.caption: Pan de higo from Málaga province—pressed fig-and-almond cake beside mountain cheese.
fig-med-35.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Pan de higo.jpg (CC BY 2.0).

fig-med-36.alt: Turkish incir dolması dried figs stuffed with walnuts
fig-med-36.caption: İncir dolması—opened dried figs stuffed with walnut on an Anatolian tea table.

fig-med-37.alt: Lebanese teen matboukh fig preserve in a jar
fig-med-37.caption: Teen matboukh—the paddle, the pot, sesame on the jar of Levantine fig jam.

fig-med-38.alt: Levantine fruit molasses syrup in a jar
fig-med-38.caption: Dibs teen—slow Levantine fruit molasses (dibs) in the pantry; fig and date syrups poured beside tahini and bread.
fig-med-38.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Dates syrup.jpg (illustrative for dibs teen).

fig-med-39.alt: Provençal fig and walnut tart with juice on the tin
fig-med-39.caption: Tarte aux figues—Provençal summer tart, slightly collapsed crust, goat cheese and honey in the filling.
fig-med-39.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Fig and walnut tart.jpg.

fig-med-40.commons: File:Queijo de figo (Vila Nova de Portimão, Portugal).jpg
fig-med-40.alt: Algarve queijo de figo pressed fig and almond cake
fig-med-40.caption: Algarve figos secos—Inland Loulé country queijo de figo and dried-fig trade (Portimão region).
fig-med-40.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Queijo de figo, Portugal.

fig-med-41.alt: Sardinian sapa saba grape must reduction with figs
fig-med-41.caption: Sapa di fichi—Sardinian must reduction (saba) pot for figs in wine-country kitchens before pecorino.

fig-med-42.alt: Greek glyko tou koutaliou spoon sweet fig in syrup
fig-med-42.caption: Glyko tou koutaliou—Greek spoon-sweet service with syrup, spoon, and water glass (visino shown; syko fig variant on Cypriot tables).
fig-med-42.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Gliko toy koytalioy visino.jpg (CC — check file page).

fig-med-43.alt: Maghreb couscous platter with lamb and dried fruits
fig-med-43.caption: Maghreb couscous with lamb—dried fig against grain and meat on a Casablanca table, not fine-dining smear.

fig-med-44.commons: File:William James Müller - Cairo Bazaar - B1984.23 - Yale Center for British Art.jpg
fig-med-44.alt: Khan el-Khalili bazaar in Cairo with dried goods
fig-med-44.caption: Egyptian winter teen markets—Cairo Khan el-Khalili lanes where dried figs and nuts move in winter.

fig-med-45.commons: File:Hint inciri - Indian fig - Opuntia ficus-indica 02.JPG
fig-med-45.alt: Prickly pear Opuntia fruit labeled Indian fig
fig-med-45.alt_secondary: Common fig Ficus carica fruit for comparison
fig-med-45.caption: Not the prickly pear—Opuntia ficus-indica (bajtra / fico d’India) beside true Ficus carica; the market confusion this essay resolves.
fig-med-45.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Opuntia and İncir comparison photos.

fig-med-46.alt: Mediterranean cheese plate with dried figs and pan de higo
fig-med-46.caption: Cheese plates and figs—Manchego, kaşar, and smokvenjak partners on a named three-object plate.

fig-med-47.alt: Roman Herculaneum fresco still life with two figs and a loaf of bread
fig-med-47.caption: Herculaneum MAN 8625—two figs and a loaf on a sill; Roman bread-and-fig foodway in Fourth Style (photo CC BY-SA 4.0; fresco PD).
fig-med-47.credit: ArchaiOptix CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons; wall painting public domain.

fig-med-48.alt: Turkish incir uyutması fig pudding with walnuts
fig-med-48.caption: İncir uyutması—Anatolian dried-fig dessert service; hoşaf-style compote with figs, walnuts, and milk-pudding cousin on Turkish tables.
fig-med-48.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Turkish_hosaf.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0, E4024); illustrative for uyutması service.
